sections.h2: Where the Muskingum County recorder is
sections.html:
Find the recorder at 401 Main Street, Zanesville, OH 43701. For mail, use P.O. Box 2333, Zanesville, OH 43702. You can phone (740) 455-7107. The office keeps weekday hours from half past eight until half past four and shuts for legal holidays.

The files start in 1803, a year ahead of the county's own organization in 1804. Surveyors, genealogists, attorneys and title examiners all use them.

sections.h2: How far back the online indexes go
sections.html:
Not every record type was indexed from the same year, so a search that returns nothing may only mean you are looking before the index begins. A Historical Indexes tab covers earlier material.

Online index start years by record type
Record typeIndex begins
Deeds1977
Mortgages1976
Liens and miscellaneous1975
Leases1981
Military discharges1965
Plats1800
UCC filings1993

For anything older than those years, use the Historical Indexes tab, and look at the training sheet in the office's Forms section for instructions.

Nearly every paper that touches land is on the recorder's list. Sellers and heirs most often see the following.

  • Deeds of four types: warranty, quit claim, survivorship and sheriff's.
  • Mortgages and the papers that travel with them, including releases, assignments, assumptions, subordinations and waivers of priority.
  • Land contracts, leases and easements, along with powers of attorney.
  • Trust papers, affidavits and certificates of transfer.
  • Mechanic's liens, notices of commencement, and federal or personal tax liens.

Plats, condominiums, street name changes, zoning resolutions and name changes sit on the same list.

sections.h2: What happens before a deed reaches the recorder
sections.html:
The auditor sets the route. You may deliver a document in person, mail it, or submit it through eRecording software. A description written in metes and bounds, or one covering anything short of a whole subdivision lot, needs approval first from the County Engineer's Office, third floor of the courthouse. Next stop is the Auditor's Office for the transfer. The recorder comes last.

A whole subdivision lot can skip the engineer. Notarization is required on every deed and related document, by a notary registered with the Ohio Secretary of State.

sections.h2: A walk through a typical Muskingum County sale
sections.html:
Seeing the whole route once makes each office's role clearer.

  1. An attorney or title agent writes the deed. If the description is in metes and bounds, or the parcel is not a whole subdivision lot, it is sent up to the County Engineer's Office before anything else.
  2. The seller signs before a notary on the Secretary of State's registry.
  3. Next the deed and the statement of value go to the Auditor's Office, where the seller pays the conveyance and transfer fees.
  4. Stamped by the auditor, the deed is recorded at 401 Main Street and the recording fee is paid.
  5. Your lender then records a release of the old mortgage, and the buyer gives the treasurer a new tax mailing address.

When an office rejects a paper, call that office to learn why. Drafting and correcting are not recorder jobs, so rewrites go back to your attorney.

Expect a conveyance fee of $4.00 per thousand of the sale price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, plus a $0.50 per parcel transfer fee, both payable to the auditor. State law brackets the amount. Section 319.54(G)(3) requires $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars, whichever is greater, and section 322.02 lets commissioners add an optional tax of up to thirty cents per hundred.

The seller, called the grantor, owes these charges when the deed is delivered, under section 319.202. On the statement of value filed with the deed, the seller reports any owner-occupancy tax reduction or agricultural valuation attached to the parcel.

sections.h2: What Ohio charges to record a deed
sections.html:
Recording charges are set by section 317.32: $17 base plus $17 housing trust fund for pages one and two, then $4 plus $4 per added page. Up to five dollars more may be tacked on for document preservation.

A certified copy is $1 plus $1 per page, and a seal on the certification adds 50 cents plus 50 cents. Electronic filers may pay after presentation by funds transfer or something similar. Which surcharge the county applies is a question for the recorder, so ask before writing your check.

sections.h2: Transfers exempt from the conveyance fee
sections.html:
Section 319.54(G)(3) exempts many transfers. These are the ones sellers and heirs hit most.

  • Gifts between husband and wife, or from parent to child.
  • Deeds that only confirm or fix an earlier recorded deed.
  • Court-ordered transfers, unless the court ordered a sale.
  • Transfers among heirs of one decedent where no money changes hands.
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust.
  • Interests valued at $100 or less.

Whatever exemption you claim, the statement of value has to give the reason.

Two free alert tools exist. The recorder offers Property Check, a fraud alert system that warns you about filings made on your behalf. You can also call the auditor at (740) 455-7109, option 1, to have your phone number attached to your parcels so you hear when one appears on a deed to be transferred.

Anyone who suspects the ownership record has been changed should phone the auditor at that same number. The auditor will investigate the property record and coordinate with the proper authorities if needed.

sections.h2: Muskingum County housing at a glance
sections.html: The county seat is Zanesville, and the Muskingum River cuts the county nearly in half. Population was 86,410 in 2020. Housing units total 38,597, owners live in 68.2% of occupied homes and the median owner-occupied value is $182,200. Roughly a third of occupied homes are rentals, which means plenty of sellers are landlords with tenants in the house.

After indexing, a deed appears in the online records, which are refreshed every weekday. Allow until later in the week for a deed recorded this morning to turn up in a search.

Do two things afterward. One: check the auditor's property search to see that the owner name and tax mailing address updated. Because a billing address change takes a written, signed form to the treasurer, a buyer who wants bills elsewhere should send one. Two: if a mortgage was paid off at closing, look in the mortgage index for the lender's release, which the lender must record within ninety days under section 5301.36.

Any deed provision that restricts the sale, rental or use of a dwelling because of race or color is invalid under federal law and cannot be enforced, which comes up when you read very old deeds from the county's long record.

Order matters: engineer approval when the description calls for it, then the auditor's transfer and fee, then the recorder. Selling for cash leaves that order alone but takes a buyer's lender out of the schedule. A title agent can cover every stop. Cash Home Buyers CA can list the papers to have ready so the counter does not send anything back. Bring your photo ID and any prior deed you have, and keep the recorded copy when it comes back.

faqs.a: Weekdays from half past eight until half past four, closed on legal holidays. Call (740) 455-7107.

faqs.q: Where do I send a deed in Muskingum County?
faqs.a: Start at the Auditor's Office for the transfer, then go to the recorder at 401 Main Street, Zanesville. A metes and bounds description needs County Engineer approval before the auditor will accept it.
$4.00 per thousand of price, rounded to the nearest ten cents, and $0.50 for each parcel. The seller pays at the auditor's office.
Yes, but the deed index starts in 1977. Older records are in the Historical Indexes tab on the recorder's site, which has its own training sheet.

faqs.q: Does the county offer a fraud alert for my property?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder runs a free service called Property Check, and the auditor will add your phone number to your parcels if you call (740) 455-7109 and choose option 1.
